title: What is a degree for?
summary:

The post What is a degree for? appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Paul D. Sweeney, former Chief Strategy Officer at Unite Group, current author and strategic advisor.

Before deciding whether university is worth the price, it would help to know what is being sold. ‘What is a degree for?’ ought to be a straightforward question – British universities have had several centuries to consider it – yet the answer changes depending on whether you ask a student, a parent, an employer or the university.

A degree is expected to provide knowledge, unlock professions, signal ability to employers, create a network, establish independence, deliver a social life, allow time for exploration and confer status. Somewhere in the package, the student is also expected to become an adult. The prospectus is suitably vague about how this metamorphosis is delivered.

Universities put one price on this bundle and call it ‘the university experience’. Student and parent can support the same purchase while imagining different products: independence and three interesting years for one; professional access and improved earnings for the other. Both can leave the open day delighted, each believing the other has agreed to the same thing.

I avoided the question when I applied to study Engineering. I was good at Maths and Science, Engineering sounded respectable and the adults approved. The admissions process established that I could obtain a place, but nobody established whether I wanted the education. I left after a year. For a while I regarded leaving as failure; in retrospect, it was my first informed decision about the degree.

The numbers are not as helpful as they first seem

The Institute for Fiscal Studies’ 2026 analysis estimated that university increased lifetime pre-tax earnings by around 20 per cent on average after adjusting for attainment and background. After taxes, student loans and study costs, however, it estimated that a quarter of graduates could be financially worse off than if they had not attended.

The 2026 HEPI and Advance HE Student Academic Experience Survey surveyed more than 10,000 full-time undergraduates. 45 per cent rated their course as good or very good value, with teaching quality the strongest driver. University remains valuable on average while leaving ample room for disappointment. An average is useful evidence, but not a prediction for the applicant at the kitchen table with five browser tabs open.

Different purchases need different evidence

Different benefits need different evidence. Professional access needs current accreditation and every recognised route into the work. Learning needs scrutiny of curriculum, teaching and assessment; an employment signal needs evidence from employers; a network needs repeated useful contact, not an alumni logo. Many universities already publish information about teaching, assessment, placements and outcomes. The weakness is inconsistent presentation and a loose connection between claim and evidence. A course-level percentage based on 12 respondents moves by more than eight percentage points when one answer changes. A decimal point would not make it more reliable.

The decision before the application

Schools and colleges should create a decision stage before applicants rank institutions. In it a student and their parent/carer would be supported to each record what university is expected to provide; which benefits are essential; what evidence would show that a course delivers them; and the strongest realistic alternative. They should answer separately before comparing notes.

The aim is not to force agreement but to expose assumptions. If the student is buying independence while the parent believes they are financing professional access, it is useful to discover this before accommodation deposits are due. Two written answers may reveal more than another family tour of a photogenic library.

The comparison must use credible alternatives. ‘I could always get an apprenticeship’ is no more a plan than ‘I will go to a good university’. A real alternative has names, dates, entry requirements, costs and a next step. Compare the degree with the best available option, not imaginary unemployment.

Schools and colleges could run this at the start of guidance, before course search hardens into a shortlist. UCAS could reinforce the sequence in its advice and online journey: test the route first, then search for courses. Universities could answer a common set of questions course by course: what students learn, the amount of direct teaching, the assessment mix, who teaches, placement participation and graduate outcomes. The evidence should show the year, cohort and sample size. That would be more useful than another generic claim and photograph of the library.

The exercise could produce three honest answers: yes, no and not yet. ‘Not yet’ is legitimate when delay is used to test a subject, experience work, improve a qualification or resolve a health or financial constraint. A seventeen-year-old need not know what they want to do for the rest of their life. The application process rewards a clean story about future ambition, even when reverse-engineered from the course choice. Uncertainty is not the problem. Spending three years and a substantial amount of money to avoid investigating it might be.

Universities should welcome this scrutiny. An applicant who knows why a course beats the alternatives is more likely to arrive with realistic expectations and reasons that belong to them. If the comparison leads elsewhere, it may prevent an expensive mismatch. We can ask whether university is worth it only after the applicant has established what they expect it to be worth.

full_text:
Bravo for Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett’s article (To state school alumni starting university, I say this: be proud of your background, 5 October). Finally someone stops tiptoeing around the truth about private schools: that they are not some kind of human right, but a form of segregation that no supposed meritocracy can counter.

When I arrived at the University of Oxford from a state comprehensive 30 years ago, I was met repeatedly with the following assumption: “Hello. Where are you from?” “Brighton”. “Ah, Roedean?”

Such questioners tended to move on when I said: “Er, no, Dorothy Stringer school.” Unlike those whose parents had paid to segregate them from the 93%, I did not have ready-made networks across Oxford’s colleges.

I found it baffling that they were not astonished, as I was, by the quadrangles, cloisters and wooden panelling. And I did not, as many of the students did, arrive with a ready supply of black-tie options. Shamefully, I changed my accent to such a degree that my mum could barely recognise me when I phoned home. It took time to be rightly proud that my parents had not bought my privileged education.

We need to be bolder in making explicit the nefarious effects of the UK’s continued defence of private schooling. Bravo to Labour for finally having added VAT on to fees. This should be a first step in addressing the impact of private schools on our society.

One point we might cheer ourselves with, meanwhile, is that state-school students perform better in their degrees than privately educated students with the same A-level grades. It seems that buying your child an advantage loses its edge once the autonomous work of university study begins.

Dr Rowan Cerys Tomlinson

Oxford

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett’s article took me back to when I was interviewed at Oxford University, where applicants had to stay in the college for a few days. I lost count of the times I was asked: “Which school do you go to?”

On the first evening having dinner, one of my fellow applicants asked everyone: “Did you board?” Conversation then turned to how many generations of everyone’s family had attended Oxford and how embarrassing it would be if they weren’t to get in (I was the first in my family to attend university).

I remember going back to my room that night feeling sick and uncomfortable, and that Oxford was not for me. I’ve since wondered whether it was bad luck that I seemed to have the worst kind of stereotypical experience.

Sadly, reading news in recent years about students at Durham, Edinburgh and St Andrews experiencing classism, it doesn’t seem like much has changed. As for me, I ended up at Warwick, which has its fair share of privileged students, but felt far more normal than what I’d witnessed at Oxford.

Elena Williams

Newcastle upon Tyne

I’m proud to have gone to a state school in Scotland, although at university, again in Scotland, I was aware of the state-private school divide. Of course, the question of “What school did you go to?” in Scotland has other connotations. It is a not-so-discreet way of trying to ascertain your religious affiliation.

Dr Harpreet S Kohli

Glasgow

title: Deadline review – shocking threat sends tremors through authoritarian school
summary:
Set in a dystopian private academy rife with surveillance and cut-throat competition, Kiwi Chow’s gripping drama cements his status as an important film-maker

Filmed in Taiwan and set entirely inside a prestigious high school, Kiwi Chow’s gripping drama frames educational systems not merely as a preparation for the real world but as a microcosm of society at large. At this elite private institute, pupils studiously march in lines like obedient soldiers, their purple uniforms the only pop of colour in a grey building of glass and steel. The school’s operations have a touch of dystopian sci-fi: students check in with AI recognition panels, which also display their class standing and disciplinary scores. In this sterile environment where human worth is measured by standardised metrics, the breathing room for individuality is nil.

This panopticon atmosphere of surveillance and cut-throat competition is punctured by a shocking incident: an anonymous student drops a flurry of leaflets announcing their intent to take their own life on the day of the final exam, unless the school changes its authoritarian ways. The note sends tremors through both the administration and the students; intersecting narrative lines weave through a group of characters that include a model student, a dedicated but ambivalent teacher and a righteous slacker. Each carries a heavy secret that points to the moral rot beneath the facade of academic excellence.

The note sends tremors through both the administration and the students; intersecting narrative lines weave through a group of characters that include a model student, a dedicated but ambivalent teacher and a righteous slacker. Each carries a heavy secret that points to the moral rot beneath the facade of academic excellence.

Though grappling with heavy subjects such as self-harm, bullying and drug use, Chow treats these youthful foibles as evidence of a systemic malaise rather than individual failings. A staunch anti-authoritarian message is smuggled in the conventions of a whodunnit thriller; it parallels Chow’s previous films, including the 2021 documentary Revolution of Our Times, about the 2019-2020 Hong Kong protests. Like the rebellion in Deadline, that movement also began on campuses and was led by students. That both titles are banned in Hong Kong only underscores the urgency and importance of Chow’s film-making.

full_text:
Good morning. I’m back, but don’t get too excited. I’ll just be making guest appearances here and there.

Now, onto children, who – if the steady stream of warnings is anything to go by – are in serious trouble. There’s the pull of addictive screens, a sharp drop in children reading for pleasure, a global decline in academic performance, and a notable rise in youth mental health struggles. Together, these trends point to a wider crisis in learning.

Much of the focus has been on phones and social media. A global study published last week found an association between increased screen exposure and lower academic achievement and poorer language development in children. In the UK, phones are already banned during the school day, and from spring of next year, under-16s will not be able to access major social media platforms such as TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram.

But are we focusing on the wrong thing? Today, I speak to Jenny Anderson, award-winning journalist and author of The Disengaged Teen, about why so many young people are disengaging from learning, and what it might take to turn that around. That’s after the headlines.

Weekend roundup

Ukraine | Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.

Middle East | A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people.

UK politics | Andy Burnham is facing questions over plans to speed up sweeping changes to Britain’s electoral system amid speculation that some of his closest advisers are pressing for an early general election.

Djibouti | At least 139 people, including 15 children, have died after a boat carrying 305 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.

Brexit | Andy Burnham has said it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, after seeking answers on the Kremlin’s involvement in the 2016 vote when he entered Downing Street.

In depth: ‘We’re shuffling kids through a system that feels like prison’

There is a real and growing crisis in young people’s engagement with learning.

According to recent research, fewer pupils now say they find school engaging. In 2020-21, 42% of students said they found what they learned interesting either “always/very often” or “quite often”. By 2023, that figure had fallen to just 28%. Nearly half of pupils do not take part in extracurricular activities, while severe absence – defined as missing more than 50% of school sessions – are on the rise in England.

Pupils are also becoming less happy at school. The share of pupils who say they are happy at school dropped from 65% in 2020-2021 to 50% in 2023-2024. Perhaps most strikingly, survey data suggests pupils feel worse, physically and mentally, than they did during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Jenny Anderson argues this points to something more complex than distraction from phones: a fundamental problem in how our schools are designed.

“We’re shuffling kids through a system, which they tell us feels like prison,” Anderson explains, adding that young people are “bored to tears by content that feels irrelevant to them”. The consequences of disengagement can extend beyond the classroom. “If they can’t figure themselves out as learners, they often can’t figure themselves out as people. They often don’t feel they belong.”

It’s not just the phones

Much of the debate has centred on the addictive nature of smartphones, particularly the social media platforms that dominate them.

In March, a US court found Meta and Google’s YouTube liable for deliberately designing addictive products used by millions of young people. A flurry of lawsuits against Meta followed, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, around alleged social media addiction in young users.

In August, as part of a landmark $18bn settlement, the company agreed to establish safeguards for teenage users, such as a daily usage limit of two hours and blocking social media use at night.

“Phones have done tremendous damage,” Anderson says. “They are very risky to kids because they are clearly created with pathologically addictive algorithms.”

Anderson argues that these algorithms displace the experiences kids need to build a sense of identity and purpose: time with friends, developing interests, and getting involved in their communities.

The platforms are also built around “weaponised engagement”, Anderson adds, putting them in direct competition with the slower and more difficult work of learning.

But while she welcomes the effort to rein in the damage caused by phones, she warns against treating phones as the sole issue in this education crisis.

Anderson describes technology as an “exacerbator” – one which accelerates the disengagement that is already present in schools, rather than causing it in the first place. Phones offer an easy, addictive alternative to the hard work of learning, but simply taking devices away does not automatically re-engage students.

“Focusing only on phones and tech misses the whole story. It distracts us from the conversation about what schools need to fix.”

Four learning modes

Anderson’s book investigates why so many young people dislike school, and what can be done about it. She identifies four modes in which students approach their education:

Passenger: Students who are coasting along and doing the bare minimum. This is about 50% of students.

Resister: Students who withdraw or act out. These are learners dubbed the “problem children”, but they are actually just children struggling with problems.

Achiever: Students who aim to get gold stars in everything without knowing why. They have the highest rate of mental health challenges of all the modes.

Explorer: Students who are curious, self-aware and driven. They have agency: the ability to set a goal, and the skills and will to go after it. While achievers may appear to represent the pinnacle of academic performance, Anderson argues that it’s actually the explorer mode.

These dynamic modes aren’t fixed, Anderson argues. They work in tandem with a set of variables, such as how a student feels about a subject, whether they have had breakfast that morning, or whether they’re fighting with their family.

According to her research, just 4% of children say they spend time at school in explorer mode.

“The irony is that kids who are coasting and appear to be lazy and appear not to be doing what we want often need more autonomy, not less,” Anderson says.

She points to research into what is known as “autonomy-supportive teaching”, which included 35 randomised controlled trials across 18 countries. These studies suggest that giving students greater agency, can improve both academic performance and wellbeing.

Anderson argues schools also need to adapt to how students engage with learning, particularly when the curriculum leaves pupils feeling overwhelmed and disconnected. “Students go through a packed out curriculum that culminates in preparing to sit for 25 exams over two months for their GCSEs,” she says.

Part of the answer lies in giving pupils more agency – this time in the classroom. Rather than assigning every student the exact same essay, teachers could offer a choice of topics and let students pursue the angle that interests them most. The aim is not to lower standards, she argues, but to create forms of learning that compete more successfully for students’ attention.

The pressures on schools may also grow as the climate crisis intensifies. Last week Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union , said schools should consider changing start and finish times, reordering holidays and moving exams from the summer months in an effort to adapt to the UK’s increasingly severe heatwaves. His comments followed school closures during June’s heatwave, which left at least 760,000 pupils in England and Wales missing lessons.

Looking ahead

Parents looking at recent headlines about education may feel powerless, Anderson says, but she believes they have a crucial role to play in helping children stay curious and engaged outside the pressures of the classroom.

Her advice is simple: start by asking children what they’re actually interested in.

“I really do think parents play a profound role here, and I think we feel trapped,” Anderson says. “We feel like we have to play the game of the system” – focusing relentlessly on grades, exams and measurable achievement – “but the system is not serving our kids.

“So we have to ask: are we just going to shove them into that system, or help them succeed in that system while also helping them figure out who they are, what they care about, where they want to make an impact in the world?”

When asked what advice she would give to education secretary Bridget Phillipson, Anderson highlights three priorities, starting with reforming the exam timetable.

“Tests are an excellent way you figure out if kids are learning, but they do not have to be so high stakes,” she explains. “They can be adaptive.”

Her second priority is making the curriculum more relevant to pupils’ lives outside school. “Kids ask all the time, ‘Why do I have to learn this?’ and we do not honour that question,” Anderson says. Schools need to help pupils see the bigger picture.

Her third piece of advice advice would be to reinvigorate the arts and humanities.

While she understands the economic case for the “relentless pursuit of STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics)”, she believes that something vital has been lost.

“What about the humanities? What about the arts, such as drama and music?” she asks. “That is the canvas on which many kids will show up and find their place in school.”

Anderson accepts that learningmust be challenging and rigorous. But, she says, it doesn’t have to be dreary . “There’s a myth of misery, that school can only be good if it’s hard in that joyless way, and that teenagers are just [naturally] unhappy.

“To borrow a Britishism, that’s poppycock.”

The week to come

Tuesday | MPs on the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will question AI bosses on regulation, security breaches and safety concerns.

Thursday | The SNPs annual party conference kicks off in Aberdeen.

Friday | Teddy Young, the Royal Navy sailor accused of spying for Russia, is due to appear at the Old Bailey in London.

What else we’ve been enjoying

I really enjoyed Alexis Petridis’ profile of “pop’s great survivors” Duran Duran, and in particular frontman Simon Le Bon comparing the creeping prevalence of AI in music to “really bad school dinners”. Sam Coare, newsletters team

As the hostile ‘one in, one out’ scheme for refugees ends, people seeking asylum share their heartbreaking testimonies with Diane Taylor, while they wait to cross the Channel. Sundus Abdi, newsletters team

Ed Pilkington’s deep dive into the future of capital punishment in the wake of Christa Pike’s botched lethal injection – and the unimaginable plan to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution – is essential reading. Sam

Sport

Football | Manchester City beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in their first game since being found guilty on more than 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial rules.

F1 | Delivering an emphatic reminder of how imperious he can be when he has the car beneath him, Max Verstappen was untouchable in victory at the Singapore Grand Prix.

Rugby union | A hat-trick from Newcastle wing Christian Wade was not enough to stop Exeter claiming their first Gallagher Prem win of the season in a topsy-turvy game at Sandy Park.

The front pages

The Guardian splashes with “Heat pump subsidy to be cut to fund defence plan”. The Mail leads with “Boris blasts ‘sickening’ Trump deal with Putin”, the Telegraph says “Putin breaks Trump’s ‘ceasefire’” and the Financial Times has “US threatens block on Kyiv’s arms in push to halt Russian refinery attacks”. The Times leads with “Almost 2m on sickness benefit may not qualify”, the Mirror goes with “Horror at tiger park” and The i Paper has “Tax rises needed to plug £35bn gap, UK economists warn Chancellor”. Finally, the Sun goes with “BBC in strictly trans ban row”.

Today in Focus

‘Gaza is a moral tear in the universe’: Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor

Are we really living through ‘end-times fascism’? Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor think so. In a new series from the Guardian, the pair speak to Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty in an extended interview. From Trump 2.0 and the rise of the tech billionaires to Gaza and the climate emergency, Klein and Taylor argue we are not just lurching from crisis to crisis but are in a new and dangerous moment in history. But they haven’t given up hope of a fightback. You can watch the full interview with Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor here.

Cartoon of the day | Pete Songi

The Upside

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Photographer Irina Werning grew up in rural Argentina surrounded by animals. It was there that she began her project capturing images at agricultural shows – “a kind of Darwinian theatre, looking for moments when humans and animals unexpectedly mirror each other.”

Four years ago, she turned her lens towards shows across the UK. From dogs in Crocs to fancy horse competitions, Werning’s work is a “celebration of places where people still gather to see and celebrate” animals, while exploring our “changing relationship” with them “as they become less visible in the countryside”.

title: Re-Evaluate Graduate Program Structure to Meet All Students’ Needs
summary:
Re-Evaluate Graduate Program Structure to Meet All Students’ Needs sara.custer@in… Sun, 10/11/2026 - 01:14 PM

Support should go beyond financial aid. 

Byline(s)
Letters to the Editor
full_text:
To the editor,

In “4 Lessons on Lower-Income Student Success” (Oct. 6, 2026), Joshua Bay highlights how financial strain undermines students’ ability to complete higher education and outlines tangible ways institutions can better support them.

Having navigated undergraduate education in acute poverty and now contributing professionally to conversations about improving college students’ financial well-being, I found this article particularly timely and important. As a graduate student, I have encountered another gap in educational support: combined financial and structural challenges affecting graduate students, particularly those in programs with limited assistantship and funding opportunities.

Graduate students may struggle with food and housing insecurity, inadequate health care, transportation costs, and other basic expenses while navigating demanding academic programs that leave little time for paid employment. As a master of social work student, I am balancing a full-time course load, an unpaid mandatory practicum internship and commutes of up to 90 minutes each way to both campus and to my practicum placement. Despite using federal loans that covered tuition and fees and little else, I have had to take a part-time job that barely covers transportation and groceries.

The resulting physical and psychological exhaustion are not simply personal challenges; they reflect an educational structure that often assumes students can afford to prioritize school over paid work. For graduate students who might have to choose between attending class, affording gas and working to cover basic expenses, emergency aid may offer some temporary relief. However, additional applications and paperwork create yet another burden for students already struggling to stay afloat.

Institutions should build on Bay’s recommendations by addressing a fifth issue: re-evaluating graduate program structure. While my experience is specific to social work education, the broader concern extends to accredited graduate programs across disciplines. The goal is not to lower academic standards, but to ensure programs are structured and delivered in ways that are educationally effective, equitable and sustainable for students.

Accreditation standards establish fundamental educational requirements, but institutions and faculty retain responsibility for how those standards are implemented. This includes evaluating the volume and sequencing of coursework and assignments, coordinating deadlines and course content to reduce repetitive overlap and unnecessary textbook costs, and reconsidering whether the cumulative demands of a two-year program are realistic for students who must also work to support themselves today.

Programs requiring internships, such as social work, should examine the financial and logistical burdens of unpaid practicum placements, including transportation costs and lengthy commutes.

Re-evaluating these structures does not mean compromising educational rigor; however, it does mean ensuring that the way graduate students are expected to meet those standards is intentional, effective and attainable for students across economic circumstances. Higher education cannot promise opportunity while structuring degree completion around the assumption that students have financial support elsewhere. If graduate programs want students from lower-income backgrounds to succeed and serve their communities, especially in fields like social work, they must make education sustainable throughout the degree and not merely accessible at admission.

title: AI in Teacher Preparation: Why Student Privacy Must Come First
summary:

The post AI in Teacher Preparation: Why Student Privacy Must Come First appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
Artificial Intelligence has rapidly entered teacher preparation programs. Preservice teachers are increasingly using generative AI tools to brainstorm lesson ideas, differentiate instruction, create assessments, draft parent communication, and generate instructional materials (Celik, Dindar, & Jarvela, 2022; Tunjera & Chigona, 2025). In many ways, this shift mirrors earlier waves of educational technology integration: the tools arrive quickly, enthusiasm grows rapidly, and educators work to determine how these technologies can meaningfully support teaching and learning within their individual environments (Cuban, 2018; Violanti, 2023).

But amid this enthusiasm surrounding AI, one issue deserves far more attention in teacher preparation programs: student privacy.

Many preservice teachers have little experience navigating the legal and ethical responsibilities surrounding student data. As a result, they may unknowingly enter personally identifiable information (PII) into public AI systems without understanding the implications. Teacher education programs therefore face an important challenge to not simply teach future educators how to use AI, but to help them understand when AI use becomes inappropriate, unethical, or potentially unlawful within K-12 settings.

The conversation surrounding AI in education cannot focus solely on efficiency or innovation, it must also center on professional responsibility.

The Problem Many Preservice Teachers Do Not Recognize

Today’s teacher candidates are often highly comfortable with digital tools. However, assumptions that they fully understand the implications of these tools are often unfounded (Bennett & Maton, 2010) . Many already use AI informally before entering methods courses or field placements. They may use chatbots to summarize readings, generate discussion questions, or revise writing. Because these tools feel conversational and accessible, it is easy for students to forget that AI platforms are still data systems. This creates a significant concern in teacher preparation that is not being addressed (Tunjera & Chigona, 2025) .

Consider a few common scenarios:

A preservice teacher uploads a struggling student’s writing sample into an AI chatbot and asks for feedback suggestions.

A candidate enters information about a student’s learning disability while seeking differentiation ideas.

A student teacher copies behavioral concerns into an AI platform to generate a parent email draft.

A candidate uploads assessment data to help AI create small-group interventions.

In each case, the preservice teacher may believe they are trying to help students. However, they may also be disclosing protected student information into systems that have not been approved by a school district or institution. Many teacher candidates simply do not realize this is problematic.

Why This Matters in K-12 Education

K-12 educators have long held ethical and legal responsibilities surrounding student records and confidentiality. AI tools do not eliminate those responsibilities.

In New York State, Education Law §2-d establishes protections surrounding the privacy and security of student data (The New York State Senate, 2024) . Similar protections exist nationally through laws such as the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) (Education, 1974) . While teacher candidates do not need to become legal experts, they do need to understand an important principle:

Student information should never be entered into AI systems without careful consideration of privacy, district policy, appropriate legislation, and platform protections.

The challenge is that many public AI tools are not designed specifically for K-12 educational compliance. Some platforms may store prompts, use uploaded information for system improvement, or lack safeguards expected in school environments. Even when names are removed, contextual details may still make students identifiable, particularly in small schools, communities, or specialized classroom environments.

Teacher education programs therefore face a significant task: helping future educators understand not only how to use AI, but when its use may become inappropriate, unethical, or even unlawful in K–12 settings.

Moving Beyond “How to Prompt”

Much of the current AI conversation in higher education focuses on prompting techniques and workflow strategies (Celik, Dindar, & Jarvela, 2022; Lucas, Bem-haja, Zhang, Llorente-Cejudo, & Palacios-Rodriguez, 2025). Those conversations are useful, but they are incomplete. Preservice teachers also need explicit instruction in ethical AI use. Teacher preparation programs should begin discussing questions such as:

What information should never be entered into an AI system?

What counts as personally identifiable information?

How do district-approved AI tools differ from public platforms?

When should AI not be used at all?

How can educators protect student confidentiality while still benefiting from AI-supported instructional planning?

These conversations are increasingly essential components of professional preparation. If we teach preservice teachers only how to use AI tools, but not how to evaluate them responsibly, we risk normalizing unsafe instructional habits before candidates even enter the profession.

Practical Ways Teacher Educators Can Address Student Privacy

Fortunately, teacher educators do not need to redesign entire programs to begin addressing these concerns. Small instructional shifts can make a significant difference.

1. Model Safe AI Practices During Instruction

Faculty should consistently demonstrate responsible use when modeling AI tools within class. For example:

Use fictional student examples instead of real cases.

Remove identifying details from classroom scenarios.

Demonstrate how to redact information before using AI tools.

Explain why certain information should never be uploaded.

These small modeling decisions communicate professional expectations clearly and consistently.

One simple strategy is encouraging preservice teachers to ask themselves a short series of questions before uploading any materials to AI:

Does this contain identifiable student information?

Would I be comfortable sharing this publicly?

Is this tool approved by a district or institution?

Am I protecting student dignity and confidentiality?

Could this information unintentionally identify a child?

Building this reflective pause into coursework helps future educators develop habits of professional judgment rather than impulsive use of technology.

3. Incorporate AI Ethics into Assignments and Discussions

Teacher educators can integrate ethical reflection into existing coursework without sacrificing instructional time. For example:

Have students analyze AI-use scenarios for ethical concerns.

Ask candidates to identify unsafe prompting practices.

Include privacy considerations within lesson-planning assignments.

Discuss how AI intersects with professional teaching standards.

These discussions help candidates recognize that technology integration is not simply technical but also grounded in pedagogy and ethics.

4. Emphasize District Policies and Approved Platforms

Many preservice teachers assume all AI tools function similarly. They often do not understand that districts may have approved platforms with specific privacy agreements in place, a practice mandated for example, by NY Education Law §2-d. Teacher education programs should therefore help candidates understand:

The importance of district policies.

Approved educational tools.

Data protection expectations.

Professional accountability during field placements.

This is especially important as school districts continue to develop their own AI guidelines and policies.

5. Frame Student Privacy as an Issue of Trust

Perhaps most importantly, teacher educators should frame student privacy as more than compliance. At its core, protecting student information is about trust. Families trust educators with sensitive academic, health, behavioral, and personal information. Students trust teachers to handle their experiences responsibly and professionally. AI does not diminish that obligation. Rather, the rapid growth of AI tools makes this relationship of trust and corresponding ethical decision-making even more critical. Future educators must understand that innovation should never come at the expense of student dignity or confidentiality.

Preparing Teachers for Responsible AI Integration

AI will almost certainly remain a growing part of K-12 education, and teacher preparation programs have a critical opportunity to shape how future educators approach those tools. The goal should not be fear or avoidance. AI can absolutely support creativity, differentiation, organization and reformative instructional design. But responsible integration requires more than technological fluency, it requires appropriate professional judgment.

As colleges and universities prepare future teachers for AI-enhanced classrooms, student privacy cannot become an afterthought. Long after candidates forget the perfect prompt structure on the latest AI platform, they must remember a far more important lesson: each technological decision educators make should protect the trust, dignity, and well-being of the students they serve.

Dr. Richard J. Violanti is an assistant professor in the College of Education at Niagara University. He holds a PhD in Curriculum, Instruction, and the Science of Learning from SUNY Buffalo, where his research examined how teachers integrate technology using the TPACK and SAMR Frameworks.

Before joining higher education, he spent more than 31 years as a secondary social studies teacher, department chair, and instructional technology leader in New York State public schools. During that time, he led curriculum redesign initiatives, supported district technology adoption, and facilitated professional learning communities focused on instructional design and ethical technology use.

At Niagara University, Dr. Violanti teaches foundations and pedagogy courses and works to integrate AI literacy and student-centered technology practices into teacher preparation. His work focuses on helping instructors use emerging technologies in ways that strengthen relationships, deepen learning, and support all students.

title: Giovani e senior, le politiche per vincere la sfida del lavoro
summary: C’è chi sta rafforzando la formazione in ingresso dei giovani talenti, affiancati dal personale senior. Chi sta trattenendo profili prossimi alla pensione per non disperdere il patrimonio di conoscenze e...
full_text:
C’è chi sta rafforzando la formazione in ingresso dei giovani talenti, affiancati dal personale senior. Chi sta trattenendo profili prossimi alla pensione per non disperdere il patrimonio di conoscenze e competenze specialistiche acquisite negli anni. E ancora: c’è chi prova strumenti, anche innovativi, per accompagnare le transizioni professionali, mantenendo alta competitività e innovazione. Perché, se è vero che prepensionamenti e misure, più o meno volontarie, del passato per favorire gli esodi del personale sono oggi economicamente poco sostenibili; è altrettanto vero che il mondo del lavoro sta cambiando e le aziende sono impegnate a sperimentare forme nuove di organizzazione, con una base in comune: valorizzare i contributi di tutti, giovani e senior. È quanto emerso durante la tappa di Bologna del roadshow dedicato alla Cultura d’impresa, organizzata da 4Manager e dal Gruppo Il Sole 24 Ore.

«I cambiamenti al centro del mondo del lavoro sono un tema importante per le nostre imprese - ha sottolineato Tiziana Ferrari, Dg di Confindustria Emilia -. Per questo, come Confindustria Emilia Area Centro da tempo stiamo affrontando con grande attenzione molte nuove esigenze, tra cui quella dell’allungamento della vita professionale e del ricambio professionale e imprenditoriale, dedicando tempo ed energie alla formazione di tutte le leve all’interno dell’azienda, sotto i più vari aspetti. Riteniamo che quelli che si possono leggere come problemi, se affrontati con i giusti strumenti e la giusta motivazione possano fare, per ogni azienda, la vera differenza». Sulla stessa lunghezza d’onda Paola Boromei, Chief Operating Officer Gruppo Il Sole 24 ORE: «Le distanze tra generazioni si chiudono quando le competenze circolano. Team intergerazionali e mentoring reciproco fanno incontrare l’esperienza di chi conosce l’impresa con i nuovi linguaggi digitali. La tecnologia accelera il lavoro, ma il giudizio si costruisce tra persone. Per questo il passaggio decisivo non riguarda solo il savoir-faire, ma anche il savoir-être. È lì che la pluralità generazionale diventa vantaggio competitivo».

Un messaggio condiviso anche da Elena Bonetti, presidente Commissione parlamentare di inchiesta sugli effetti economici e sociali derivanti dalla transizione demografica in atto: «Avere più generazioni al lavoro non basta: il vantaggio nasce quando l’esperienza degli uni diventa una leva per la crescita e l’innovazione degli altri». Del resto, «l’invecchiamento della forza lavoro richiede alle imprese di investire nelle persone lungo tutta la vita professionale - ha spiegato Claudio Lucifora, ordinario di economia politica all’università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore -. Formazione continua, scambio di competenze tra generazioni e contrasto agli stereotipi sull’età aiutano a valorizzare l’esperienza dei lavoratori senior e a sostenere la produttività».

Il punto, come ha ricordato Paolo Sestito, Capo del Dipartimento Pianificazione, Organizzazione e Bilancio della Banca d’Italia, è che «l’insostenibilità economica dei pensionamenti precoci è ormai accettata. Il tema oggi è come valorizzare la convivenza di più generazioni in azienda, agendo su incentivi diversi dagli automatismi retributivi e dalle prospettive di una lunga carriera interna, in prospettiva poco credibili in quanto causa di rigidità e d’un dualismo generazionale. Serve puntare su valori che possano accomunare. Ma per non cadere nella retorica, serve dare un sostrato materiale a tale convivenza e una via può venire dallo sfruttamento dell’AI, con un approccio operativo per team e strutture organizzative meno rigide». D’accordo Alice Pretto, presidente di Essay Group e vicepresidente dei GI di Confindustria: «La pluralità generazionale funzionerà davvero quando nessuna generazione sentirà di dover chiedere il permesso all’altra per avere valore. Quando l’esperienza diventerà un patrimonio da condividere e le nuove prospettive troveranno spazio per contribuire alla crescita dell’impresa. Ogni generazione porta con sé competenze, sensibilità e modi diversi di interpretare il proprio tempo. La sfida è imparare a riconoscere il valore dell’altro, anche quando prende forme diverse da quelle che conosciamo. È da questa consapevolezza che può nascere una responsabilità condivisa: mettere ciò che siamo e ciò che sappiamo a disposizione di quello che ancora possiamo costruire». Per Gaia Giappichelli, Commissione Nazionale Hr Federmanager e Industrial Relations Nexi, è importante ribadire come Federmanager stia implementando nuovi percorsi sul fronte della management dei lavoratori senior in agenda e, da esponente del settore del credito - settore di per sé ricco e dunque propenso ad accordi di accompagnamento in uscita dei lavoratori - , evidenzia come «nell’ambito della discussione sul nuovo contratto di settore si sta esaminando la possibilità di introdurre strumenti a sostegno di percorsi per la valorizzazione dei dipendenti senior nelle aziende».

A curare le conclusioni dell’appuntamento è Francesca Mazzolari, direttrice generale di 4Manager, che fissa le priorità in campo: «L’uscita anticipata dei lavoratori non solo non è più sostenibile dal punto di vista macroeconomico, ma è anche poco vantaggioso per le aziende. Le imprese che investono in Age management hanno ritorni in termini di produttività, ma servono strumenti legislativi e politiche pubbliche». Tra le proposte avanzate da 4Manager dopo una fase di confronto con una quarantina di imprese, c’è quella della Staffetta delle competenze, che superi i meccanismi dell’attuale Staffetta generazionale. «La condizione per ottenere gli incentivi deve essere quella di strutturare passaggi di competenze tra lavoratori senior e junior», ha concluso Mazzolari.

title: Denaro è libertà: come negoziare il proprio valore sul lavoro
summary:
Costruire il proprio potere finanziario sul posto di lavoro e nella vita quotidiana richiede il superamento di tabù storici, strategie di negoziazione efficaci e un piano chiaro per la gestione consapevole dei propri guadagni

L'articolo Denaro è libertà: come negoziare il proprio valore sul lavoro proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
Il rapporto con il denaro definisce in modo profondo l’autonomia individuale e le dinamiche professionali nella società contemporanea, eppure rimane uno degli argomenti meno affrontati e più carichi di ansia. In un’intervista rilasciata al podcast Fixable, condotto dalle esperte di gestione aziendale Anne Morriss e Frances Frei, la divulgatrice ed educatrice finanziaria Haley Sacks, nota come Mrs. Dow Jones e autrice del volume Future Rich Person: The New Tools for Building Wealth, ha analizzato le dinamiche fondamentali per sviluppare un reale potere finanziario. L’analisi affronta il legame tra capitale, libertà decisionale e carriera, fornendo indicazioni per gestire le proprie risorse ed eliminare i blocchi emotivi legati all’ambito economico.

Il legame tra capitale e libertà decisionale

La disponibilità di risorse economiche rappresenta prima di tutto uno strumento di emancipazione e di tutela della propria indipendenza. Come spiegato da Sacks, raggiungere il potere finanziario significa estendere il ventaglio delle opzioni a propria disposizione nella vita di tutti i giorni. Sacks sottolinea la natura di questo legame affermando: “Il denaro, la libertà e il potere hanno molto a che fare con il semplice fatto di poter dire la propria sulla propria vita. E penso che siamo tutti d’accordo sul fatto che quando abbiamo denaro, abbiamo opzioni”.

Questa capacità di scelta diventa determinante quando si presenta la necessità di sottrarsi a contesti lavorativi o personali svalutanti. L’autonomia economica offre la forza contrattuale necessaria per rifiutare condizioni inaccettabili. A questo proposito, Sacks dichiara: “Abbiamo il potere di allontanarci da situazioni che non ci servono, se odiamo il nostro capo o stiamo vivendo una brutta relazione, o una qualsiasi di queste cose che possono davvero bloccarci”. Sfatare l’idea che il capitale sia slegato dalla qualità della vita è un altro punto centrale dell’analisi.

Sebbene le risorse economiche non garantiscano automaticamente il benessere emotivo, Sacks nota: “E sai, la gente dice sempre che i soldi non danno la felicità, ma guarda, i soldi non hanno mai reso nessuno meno felice”. In merito al rapporto tra reddito e soddisfazione personale, la docente Frei ha ricordato che le ricerche scientifiche evidenziano una correlazione positiva che tende a stabilizzarsi attorno alla soglia dei 100.000 dollari annui, cifra oltre la quale l’impatto del reddito incrementale sulla felicità si appiattisce.

L’emancipazione economica e il contesto storico

Il denaro rimane uno degli argomenti più complessi da affrontare apertamente. Secondo i dati citati da Sacks, le questioni finanziarie figurano al secondo posto tra i temi che le persone evitano di discutere, subito dopo il sesso e la morte. Questa riservatezza genera isolamento e impedisce lo scambio di informazioni essenziali, come il confronto sui salari o sui piani di risparmio per la pensione, condizionando in modo particolare le donne.

Dal punto di vista storico, l’opportunità per la popolazione femminile di gestire la propria ricchezza è una conquista recente. Negli Stati Uniti, le donne non hanno potuto ottenere una carta di credito a proprio nome fino al 1974, né richiedere un prestito aziendale autonomo fino agli anni ’80. Sacks evidenzia l’importanza di questo percorso storico dichiarando: “Siamo davvero le prime generazioni di donne che hanno il controllo sulla propria vita, il potere di scegliere e il potere di prendere un pennello e fare della tela della propria vita qualsiasi cosa vogliamo”.

Trasformare la mentalità finanziaria e gestire il patrimonio

Molte persone considerate competenti nel proprio lavoro manifestano insicurezze quando si tratta di gestire le proprie finanze. Morriss e Frei hanno evidenziato come l’assenza di un’educazione finanziaria formale provochi spesso un bagaglio di vergogna legato agli errori passati o alla sensazione di sprecare le proprie risorse.

Sacks chiarisce che la competenza economica non costituisce una dote innata, ma una disciplina che può essere appresa mediante la matematica di prima media e l’automazione dei processi.

I passaggi operativi per la sicurezza economica

Per costruire un potere finanziario solido, la salute economica deve integrarsi con il benessere fisico ed emotivo. L’approccio strutturato da Sacks individua una sequenza precisa di interventi: comprendere prima di tutto i propri blocchi emotivi, accumulare successivamente un fondo di emergenza pari a 3-6 mesi di spese all’interno di un conto di deposito ad alto rendimento (High-Yield Savings Account), saldare i debiti ad alto interesse e infine massimizzare i contributi verso i conti con agevolazioni fiscali, come i piani pensionistici IRA e 401(k).

A questo schema si affianca il Piano di Spesa Future Rich Person, ideato da Sacks per bilanciare la pianificazione del futuro con le spese del presente. Il modello suggerisce di destinare il 20% del reddito agli investimenti e al risparmio, riservando contemporaneamente il 30% delle entrate alle uscite personali a libera discrezione. In merito a questo bilanciamento, Sacks specifica: “Nessuna vergogna, purché tu stia pagando prima te stessa e mettendo soldi per la tua “futura persona ricca”. Non mi importa cosa fai con il resto di quei soldi”.

Affermare il proprio valore sul posto di lavoro

Sul piano professionale, la costruzione del potere finanziario richiede la capacità di creare valore all’interno dell’organizzazione per poi catturarlo in termini retributivi. Durante la discussione, Frei ha rimarcato come le aziende e i singoli professionisti debbano focalizzarsi sulla crescita delle entrate piuttosto che sul solo contenimento delle uscite: mentre il taglio delle spese presenta un limite naturale, il potenziale di guadagno non possiede un tetto massimo.

La strategia di negoziazione BATNA e le leve salariali

Nelle trattative contrattuali o nelle richieste di aumento di stipendio, occorre considerare leve che vanno oltre la sola retribuzione base. Sacks suggerisce di applicare il principio del BATNA (Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement), individuando alternative negoziali dotate di alto valore.

Tra gli elementi accessori da negoziare rientrano una qualifica professionale superiore (job title), giorni aggiuntivi di lavoro da casa per abbattere i costi e i tempi di spostamento, oppure il finanziamento di corsi di formazione e certificazioni. Qualora l’azienda non possa concedere un aumento immediato, è necessario fissare criteri chiari per i mesi successivi. Sacks raccomanda di impostare il confronto ponendo una domanda precisa: “E quali sono i KPI, gli indicatori chiave di prestazione, che devo raggiungere per ottenere poi quell’aumento?”. Se gli obiettivi concordati vengono raggiunti nell’arco di sei mesi ma l’azienda non concede l’adeguamento economico, la scelta strategica consiste nel valutare nuove opportunità professionali.

La trappola dei costi sommersi e la portabilità delle competenze

Un ostacolo frequente nello sviluppo della carriera è la trappola dei costi sommersi (sunk cost fallacy), che spinge a rimanere in contesti sottopagati solo per via degli anni già investiti. Sacks analizza questo errore affermando: “penso che la mossa di carriera più costosa che possiamo fare non sia cambiare lavoro, ma trascorrere un altro decennio in quello sbagliato solo perché ci hai già passato un decennio”.

In merito alla mobilità lavorativa, Frei ha richiamato le ricerche condotte dal docente di Harvard Boris Groysberg sulla portabilità dei talenti (The Portability of Stars). Lo studio evidenzia come le donne ad alto rendimento che cambiano azienda tendano a mantenere elevati livelli di successo rispetto ai colleghi uomini. Questo accade perché gli uomini fanno spesso affidamento sulle reti interne dell’azienda, mentre le donne sviluppano competenze collegate a reti esterne, rendendo le proprie capacità trasferibili in nuovi contesti organizzativi.

Azioni immediate per sviluppare sicurezza finanziaria

Il consolidamento del potere finanziario non richiede interventi complessi, ma una costanza operativa. Per superare l’esitazione iniziale, Sacks suggerisce di programmare un money date, ovvero un incontro periodico con le proprie finanze della durata di dieci minuti, utile per resettare le password dei conti o verificare i bilanci personali.

La sicurezza nell’uso del capitale non precede l’azione, ma ne è la conseguenza diretta. Sacks precisa questo concetto affermando: “la sicurezza finanziaria segue l’azione finanziaria. Il rapporto con il denaro definisce in modo profondo l’autonomia individuale e le dinamiche professionali nella società contemporanea, eppure rimane uno degli argomenti meno affrontati e più carichi di ansia. In un’intervista rilasciata al podcast Fixable, condotto dalle esperte di gestione aziendale Anne Morriss e Frances Frei, la divulgatrice ed educatrice finanziaria Haley Sacks, nota come Mrs. Dow Jones e autrice del volume Future Rich Person: The New Tools for Building Wealth, ha analizzato le dinamiche fondamentali per sviluppare un reale potere finanziario. L’analisi affronta il legame tra capitale, libertà decisionale e carriera, fornendo indicazioni per gestire le proprie risorse ed eliminare i blocchi emotivi legati all’ambito economico.

Il legame tra capitale e libertà decisionale

La disponibilità di risorse economiche rappresenta prima di tutto uno strumento di emancipazione e di tutela della propria indipendenza. Come spiegato da Sacks, raggiungere il potere finanziario significa estendere il ventaglio delle opzioni a propria disposizione nella vita di tutti i giorni. Sacks sottolinea la natura di questo legame affermando: “Il denaro, la libertà e il potere hanno molto a che fare con il semplice fatto di poter dire la propria sulla propria vita. E penso che siamo tutti d’accordo sul fatto che quando abbiamo denaro, abbiamo opzioni”.

Questa capacità di scelta diventa determinante quando si presenta la necessità di sottrarsi a contesti lavorativi o personali svalutanti. L’autonomia economica offre la forza contrattuale necessaria per rifiutare condizioni inaccettabili. A questo proposito, Sacks dichiara: “Abbiamo il potere di allontanarci da situazioni che non ci servono, se odiamo il nostro capo o stiamo vivendo una brutta relazione, o una qualsiasi di queste cose che possono davvero bloccarci”. Sfatare l’idea che il capitale sia slegato dalla qualità della vita è un altro punto centrale dell’analisi.

Sebbene le risorse economiche non garantiscano automaticamente il benessere emotivo, Sacks nota: “E sai, la gente dice sempre che i soldi non danno la felicità, ma guarda, i soldi non hanno mai reso nessuno meno felice”. In merito al rapporto tra reddito e soddisfazione personale, la docente Frei ha ricordato che le ricerche scientifiche evidenziano una correlazione positiva che tende a stabilizzarsi attorno alla soglia dei 100.000 dollari annui, cifra oltre la quale l’impatto del reddito incrementale sulla felicità si appiattisce.

L’emancipazione economica e il contesto storico

Il denaro rimane uno degli argomenti più complessi da affrontare apertamente. Secondo i dati citati da Sacks, le questioni finanziarie figurano al secondo posto tra i temi che le persone evitano di discutere, subito dopo il sesso e la morte. Questa riservatezza genera isolamento e impedisce lo scambio di informazioni essenziali, come il confronto sui salari o sui piani di risparmio per la pensione, condizionando in modo particolare le donne.

Dal punto di vista storico, l’opportunità per la popolazione femminile di gestire la propria ricchezza è una conquista recente. Negli Stati Uniti, le donne non hanno potuto ottenere una carta di credito a proprio nome fino al 1974, né richiedere un prestito aziendale autonomo fino agli anni ’80. Sacks evidenzia l’importanza di questo percorso storico dichiarando: “Siamo davvero le prime generazioni di donne che hanno il controllo sulla propria vita, il potere di scegliere e il potere di prendere un pennello e fare della tela della propria vita qualsiasi cosa vogliamo”.

Trasformare la mentalità finanziaria e gestire il patrimonio

Molte persone considerate competenti nel proprio lavoro manifestano insicurezze quando si tratta di gestire le proprie finanze. Morriss e Frei hanno evidenziato come l’assenza di un’educazione finanziaria formale provochi spesso un bagaglio di vergogna legato agli errori passati o alla sensazione di sprecare le proprie risorse.

Sacks chiarisce che la competenza economica non costituisce una dote innata, ma una disciplina che può essere appresa mediante la matematica di prima media e l’automazione dei processi.

I passaggi operativi per la sicurezza economica

Per costruire un potere finanziario solido, la salute economica deve integrarsi con il benessere fisico ed emotivo. L’approccio strutturato da Sacks individua una sequenza precisa di interventi: comprendere prima di tutto i propri blocchi emotivi, accumulare successivamente un fondo di emergenza pari a 3-6 mesi di spese all’interno di un conto di deposito ad alto rendimento (High-Yield Savings Account), saldare i debiti ad alto interesse e infine massimizzare i contributi verso i conti con agevolazioni fiscali, come i piani pensionistici IRA e 401(k).

A questo schema si affianca il Piano di Spesa Future Rich Person, ideato da Sacks per bilanciare la pianificazione del futuro con le spese del presente. Il modello suggerisce di destinare il 20% del reddito agli investimenti e al risparmio, riservando contemporaneamente il 30% delle entrate alle uscite personali a libera discrezione. In merito a questo bilanciamento, Sacks specifica: “Nessuna vergogna, purché tu stia pagando prima te stessa e mettendo soldi per la tua “futura persona ricca”. Sul piano professionale, la costruzione del potere finanziario richiede la capacità di creare valore all’interno dell’organizzazione per poi catturarlo in termini retributivi. Durante la discussione, Frei ha rimarcato come le aziende e i singoli professionisti debbano focalizzarsi sulla crescita delle entrate piuttosto che sul solo contenimento delle uscite: mentre il taglio delle spese presenta un limite naturale, il potenziale di guadagno non possiede un tetto massimo.

Tra gli elementi accessori da negoziare rientrano una qualifica professionale superiore (job title), giorni aggiuntivi di lavoro da casa per abbattere i costi e i tempi di spostamento, oppure il finanziamento di corsi di formazione e certificazioni. Qualora l’azienda non possa concedere un aumento immediato, è necessario fissare criteri chiari per i mesi successivi. Sacks raccomanda di impostare il confronto ponendo una domanda precisa: “E quali sono i KPI, gli indicatori chiave di prestazione, che devo raggiungere per ottenere poi quell’aumento?”. Se gli obiettivi concordati vengono raggiunti nell’arco di sei mesi ma l’azienda non concede l’adeguamento economico, la scelta strategica consiste nel valutare nuove opportunità professionali.
